title: GHG Emissions from Tankers that Arrive at California Ports
text:
This document explores greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from tankers arriving at California ports using an AIS (Automatic Identification System)-based emissions model developed in collaboration between Environmental Markets Lab (emLab) and Global Fishing Watch (GFW). The model and methodology is described extensively here.
Tankers arriving at California could be a significant source of maritime emissions, carrying crude oil, petroleum products, liquefied natural gas (LNG), and chemicals to refineries and terminals along the California coast. This report provides a preliminary exploratory data analysis (EDA) of tanker emissions based on the GFW model, covering vessel-level emissions estimates for voyages that end at California ports.






NoteData Access



The underlying data are pulled from Google BigQuery, where emLab and Global Fishing Watch store the vessel-level emissions model. Only collaborators with GFW BigQuery access can re-run the SQL queries (see R/01_pull_bq_data.R). All other users can reproduce this analysis using the pre-downloaded CSV files in the data/ folder.

title: GHG Emissions from Tankers that Arrive at California Ports
GHG Emissions from Tankers that Arrive at California Ports
text:
2. Load Data
Here we load the tanker trip emissions data from the CSV file into R for analysis. This dataset includes vessel-level emissions estimates for voyages that end at California ports, along with associated metadata such as distance traveled, hours at sea, starting and ending ports, and more. The dataset can be directly accessed in the GitHub repo: data/tanker_trip_emissions_ending_in_california.csv.


Show code
countries_of_interest <- c("South Korea", "India")
vessel_class_of_interest <- "tanker.oil"


tanker_trip_emissions_ending_in_california <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here(params$data_file)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    from_country = countrycode::countrycode(
      from_country_iso3,
      "iso3c",
      "country.name",
      nomatch = from_country_iso3
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    country_of_interest = ifelse(
      from_country %in% countries_of_interest,
      TRUE,
      FALSE
    )
  )

# Derive the dataset's date coverage so figure captions and axes stay in sync
# with whatever model version was pulled, rather than being hardcoded
data_min_date <- min(tanker_trip_emissions_ending_in_california$arrival_date)
data_max_date <- max(tanker_trip_emissions_ending_in_california$arrival_date)
data_date_range_label <- paste0(
  format(data_min_date, "%B %Y"),
  " through ",
  format(data_max_date, "%B %Y")
)

# The final year of data is partial unless coverage runs through December
first_year <- lubridate::year(data_min_date)
last_complete_year <- if (lubridate::month(data_max_date) == 12) {
  lubridate::year(data_max_date)
} else {
  lubridate::year(data_max_date) - 1L
}


The primary focus of the analysis is oil tankers, and on voyages departing from South Korea and India. We will explore a few figures summarizing all trips ending in California, and then filter to our vessel class and countries of interest for the remainder of the analysis.
The dataset includes 1,714 unique trips, across 739 unique tanker vessels, from 45 countries, that had arrival dates ranging from 2015-01-17 to 2026-07-31.

title: GHG Emissions from Tankers that Arrive at California Ports
text:
3. Exploratory Data Analysis
In this section, we conduct a preliminary exploratory data analysis (EDA) of the tanker trip emissions data. We will examine the distribution of emissions across voyages, identify key ports and routes, and explore potential trends in the data.
Earlier versions of the GFW model grouped crude oil tankers, petroleum product tankers, and chemical tankers together in a single tanker.chemical_oil class, and could not differentiate further. As of the v20260714 model version, oil tankers are identified as their own class, tanker.oil, and the SQL query underlying this report retrieves only that class. The tanker.oil category includes vessels classified as: Asphalt/bitumen tanker; Coal/oil mixture tanker; Crude oil tanker; Crude/oil products tanker; Products tanker; Shuttle tanker; Tanker (unspecified).
The entire analysis below therefore covers tanker.oil voyages only.


Show code
country_level_data <- tanker_trip_emissions_ending_in_california |>
  dplyr::filter(vessel_class == vessel_class_of_interest) |>
  dplyr::group_by(from_country, country_of_interest) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    total_trips = dplyr::n_distinct(trip_id),
    total_vessels = dplyr::n_distinct(ssvid),
    emissions_co2_mt = sum(emissions_co2_mt)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(-total_trips) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rank = dplyr::row_number())


Next we look at the total amount of CO2 emissions, number of tanker trips, and number of unique tanker vessels, and for all oil tanker voyages that end at California ports in our dataset, aggregated by departure country. In terms of CO2 emissions, our countries of interest, South Korea and India, rank 1 and 1 respectively out of 45 countries with voyages ending in California.
For the remainder of the analysis after this figure, we will focus on voyages departing from our countries of interest, South Korea and India.


Show code
country_level_data |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(total_trips, total_vessels, emissions_co2_mt),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric = dplyr::recode(
      metric,
      "emissions_co2_mt" = "CO2 emissions (MT)",
      "total_trips" = "Total trips",
      "total_vessels" = "Total vessels"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    y = reorder(from_country, value),
    x = value,
    fill = country_of_interest
  )) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Departure country") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1", direction = -1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma)








Figure 1: Summary of CO2 emissions, tanker trips, and unique tanker vessels, by departure country, for voyages ending at California ports. This aggregates activity from the entire time period of the dataset (January 2015 through July 2026).







Show code
# Now, filter to our countries and vessel class of interest for the remainder of the analysis
tanker_trips_of_interest_emissions_ending_in_california <- tanker_trip_emissions_ending_in_california |>
  dplyr::filter(
    vessel_class == vessel_class_of_interest,
    from_country %in% countries_of_interest
  ) |>
  # Make data spatial, using arrival port lat/lon
  sf::st_as_sf(
    coords = c("arrival_lon", "arrival_lat"),
    crs = 4326, # WGS84 coordinate reference system
    remove = FALSE
  ) # Keep original lat/lon columns


Next we look at the total amount of CO2 emissions, number of tanker trips, and number of unique tanker vessels, for oil tanker voyages that end at California ports in our dataset, aggregated by departure country and destination port. This allows us to see which California ports are receiving the most tanker traffic and emissions from our countries of interest.


Show code
port_level_data <- tanker_trips_of_interest_emissions_ending_in_california |>
  dplyr::mutate(to_port = stringr::str_to_title(to_port)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(to_port, from_country) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    total_trips = dplyr::n_distinct(trip_id),
    total_vessels = dplyr::n_distinct(ssvid),
    emissions_co2_mt = sum(emissions_co2_mt)
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(total_trips, total_vessels, emissions_co2_mt),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric = dplyr::recode(
      metric,
      "emissions_co2_mt" = "CO2 emissions (MT)",
      "total_trips" = "Total trips",
      "total_vessels" = "Total vessels"
    )
  )

port_level_data |>
  ggplot(aes(
    y = reorder(to_port, value),
    x = value,
    fill = from_country
  )) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Destination port", fill = "Departure country") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma)








Figure 2: Summary of CO2 emissions, tanker trips, and unique tanker vessels, by departure country and destination port, for oil tanker voyages that end at California ports. This aggregates activity from the entire time period of the dataset (January 2015 through July 2026).





Next we look at a map of the California arrival ports, and how much CO2 emissions are associated with tanker voyages from our countries of interest, South Korea and India, that end at each port. The size of the points corresponds to the amount of CO2 emissions (MT) from voyages departing from each country and arriving at each port.


Show code
california_land_mass <- maps::map(
  "state",
  "california",
  plot = FALSE,
  fill = TRUE
) |>
  sf::st_as_sf() |>
  sf::st_transform(crs = 3310)

ggplot() +
  # add California land mass
  geom_sf(
    data = california_land_mass,
    fill = "gray90",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = tanker_trips_of_interest_emissions_ending_in_california |>
      dplyr::mutate(to_port = stringr::str_to_title(to_port)) |>
      dplyr::group_by(to_port) |>
      dplyr::summarise(
        emissions_co2_mt = sum(emissions_co2_mt),
        geometry = sf::st_union(geometry)
      ) |> # Combine geometries for all trips to the same port
      sf::st_centroid() |> # Get centroid of each port geometry for plotting
      sf::st_transform(crs = 3310), # Transform to California Albers for better visualization,
    aes(size = emissions_co2_mt),
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "",
    y = "",
    color = "Departure country",
    size = "CO2 emissions (MT)\n from trips ending here\n(Jan 2015 to Feb 2026)"
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(3, 10),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 5),
    labels = scales::comma
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")








Figure 3: Map of California arrival ports for oil tanker voyages from South Korea and India that end at California ports. The point at each point is sized according to how much CO2 emissions occurred on trips from South Korea and India that ended in this port. This aggregates activity from the entire time period of the dataset (January 2015 through July 2026).





Next we look at a time series plot of number of tanker trips, unique tanker vessels, CO2 emissions, total hours at sea, and total distance traveled (nm), for oil tanker voyages from South Korea and India that end at California ports. We focus on the 2015-2025 period, excluding any partial final year of data. We aggregate by the year during which each voyage arrived in California.


Show code
annual_summary_data <- tanker_trips_of_interest_emissions_ending_in_california |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::filter(vessel_class == vessel_class_of_interest) |>
  dplyr::group_by(
    year = lubridate::year(arrival_date),
    from_country
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    total_trips = dplyr::n_distinct(trip_id),
    total_vessels = dplyr::n_distinct(ssvid),
    emissions_co2_mt = sum(emissions_co2_mt),
    hours = sum(hours),
    distance_nm = sum(distance_nm)
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(year <= last_complete_year) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(total_trips, total_vessels, emissions_co2_mt, hours, distance_nm),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric = dplyr::recode(
      metric,
      "emissions_co2_mt" = "CO2 emissions (MT)",
      "total_trips" = "Total trips",
      "total_vessels" = "Total vessels",
      "hours" = "Total hours at sea",
      "distance_nm" = "Total distance traveled (nm)"
    )
  )
annual_summary_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(metric ~ from_country, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "", color = "Departure country") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1", direction = -1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(first_year, last_complete_year, by = 1)) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








Figure 4: Annual number of tanker trips, unique tanker vessels, CO2 emissions, total hours at sea, and total distance traveled (nm), for oil tanker voyages from South Korea and India that end at California ports.





Here we summarize this annual data in a table


Show code
annual_summary_data |>
  dplyr::mutate(value = round(value) |> prettyNum(big.mark = ",")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = metric, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::arrange(from_country, year) |>
  knitr::kable()
